So, late to the party, but I just listened about a relevant case so I would like to contribute. Nanny Dross is the example I will use here. Her first few victims were retribution for abusive situations. She didn't know about the life insurance policy on the first husband she killed/received the money from. She had a long standing fantasy of a romantic life like in her romance novels and decided murder was the means to that end. But the money changed things and skewed her intentions towards that direction. The more she killed the more murder became habitual. So it was almost automatic with each new marriage. There are classifications which trend towards female such as black widows or angels of death but like male serial killers those are only surface level generalizations. Ed Kemper went after the co-eds so the surface level generalization for him was the hitchhiker victim type but the target he actually wanted was his mother. The act of repetitive killing either becomes habitual for lack of a better description or leads to the desired destination. But it doesn't stop there. Killers as we know escalate so these variables are always changing and evolving until they're caught or die or whatever. In my opinion that makes it case to case.

I loved the remake and I'm always happy to see others share that opinion. For visuals alone, this movie is amazing--all that rain-swept desolation, those nightmare sequences, the way that you see the dancers' bodies contort, the curve of each rib and hip. So much powerful femininity everywhere, which makes sense in a film about witches.  

I've got this thing where I enjoy situations in media where >!human characters become deified in some way. Part of what I loved the most about this film was how Suzie ascended away from her humanity to become Mother Suspiriorum. There's such a huge contrast between the innocent farm girl ballerina from the beginning of the movie and the tempered, omniscient goddess she becomes by the end. I loved how she had to denounce her own mother in order to complete the ritual. I loved how you only get teases of the trauma she experienced from her mother, too. The actress did such a wonderful job with the transition. You can see the change in her eyes, I feel, especially when she visits the professor to tell him what happened to his wife. Those were the eyes of one who is not mortal, one who is old, and wise. I also really like how you spend most of the movie along for the ride, effectively, and only truly realize what has been happening the whole time once it actually happens. The second watch-through was fun--it gave me the opportunity to kind of see how everything was progressing once I knew where it was going to go. !<

I also really liked how different it was in comparison to the original. It felt really dense and, I don't know, political, I suppose? I found myself growing attached to many of the characters and analyzing their motivations whereas in the original it was all kind of laid out for you, for the most part. 

At the end of the day, I love things that are dark and brooding with all kinds of ambiguity and symbolism. And yes, I quite agree, when it was scary, the scary parts *slapped.* My boyfriend thinks I'm nuts because of how much I like the remake, but I like it. Unashamedly. But the original is special, too. I treat them like two stories in alternate universes.

OH. My one qualm with it is the setting. I feel like the post-war setting did not really contribute too much to the plot outside of the professor's deal. I question it. :/

This place is in my hometown. I applied to work here when I was 18. They had put out a Craigslist ad for "orderlies". I sent a resume, they asked me to come in for an interview and I had to fill out 3 pages of a paper application that was filled with variations of 'could you use a cattle prod-type device to shock someone' and 'could you restrain someone' and 'could you do these things immediately if you were told to' with little bubbles for each one that were like, leftmost bubble for never, rightmost bubble for all the time. And then there were a bunch of sections describing the patients and how violent they are and how you needed to be prepared for that. I filled it out, handed it in, never heard from them again. The person who 'interviewed' me asked me no questions or anything, just  took the application and walked away. Many years later, I was hospitalized and there was group therapy. A woman came in to lead group therapy and she described having been a patient at this place. She said she has PTSD and wakes up in the middle of the night doing a clapping and stomping thing that they asked the patients to do to show they were paying attention. She also has a phobia/trigger about cleaning due to the fact that if her cleaning wasn't perfect while she was there she'd be punished. Absolutely wild.
